doc.title: Darius Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 29, 2024

title: Move to Connecticut in 1960
summary: The uprooting from Oakland to a rented house arranged through Columbia Records and Irving Townsend.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. It must have been quite a — the move to Connecticut.

Well that was a real uprooting. I remember it very clearly because it was 1960, it was a presidential year. Kennedy was elected. Kennedy ran against Nixon and won. Barry Goldwater was a big name in those days. And for me that just flags up so many historical things. But mainly what I remember was moving into a different, very different physical environment. Even Northern California is pretty arid and warm. We were in Oakland so we were, you know the prevailing vegetation was eucalyptus. You’d smell that every morning. Eucalyptus and pine and Dave and Iola had this marvelous architect-designed house which is in itself iconic. It’s near the beginning of a movement called NorCalMod — Northern California Modern — which is kind of Frank Lloyd Wright based. And you can look things up about it. I try not to go down too many tangents — follow too many tangents — but NorCalMod — to living in — renting Irving Townsend’s house on Newtown Turnpike. If you look at jazz history, recorded jazz history, he was a significant producer for Columbia Records. And Dave was just starting to break through and be a national name and moving to Connecticut was really at the behest of Columbia Records. And they wanted to send Irving Townsend to California to set up an L.A. branch, so they could offer this house, which was really nice and it was on a farm, it was kind of a rural property. Connecticut is, as you know, very humid, very green. And it was like what we called a New England salt box. You know white, with wooden shutters — excuse me I have to get some water —
